author: haiku
reason: A starts by naming the existing building blocks (log, object storage, key-value store, warehouse) and then follows one linear flow (collector, log, dedup, decided topic, archive, enrich, load, close, replay) with fewer moving parts, so a newcomer can hold the whole system in their head faster, while B's ledger, day_status table and collector fence/snapshot close make it harder to absorb even though B explains its reasons more.

author: haiku
reason: A starts with a short overview of both paths and explains why the design looks the way it does (retries, late copies, finding winners again), then holds each mechanism together end to end (idempotent upserts, the ledger, closing by log offset); B leaves gaps a newcomer would trip on, such as a loader whose appends are not idempotent and late winners that end up in both tables after a replay.

author: sonnet
reason: A starts with a clear overview just as B does, but it then lays out each component by what starts it and what data it owns, defines every term it uses, and explains the reasons behind the subtle mechanisms (the 60 s staleness bound, the checks for closing a day, the load ledger), so a newcomer gets a complete and consistent picture where B is shorter but leaves gaps such as closing days on the clock alone and a vaguer sealing rule.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains the same core design (collector, log, archive, dedup by lowest offset, closed-day fence, replay from raw) in about half the length, with the reasons stated inline and a clear opening summary, so a newcomer understands the system faster; B is more thorough but buries that understanding under extra mechanism and rollout detail.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow because each attempt restarts under its own key, so there is no checkpoint, handover or part-reuse logic to track; it groups the steps into click, job, page and failure parts, and its failure table has a column for what the user sees, while A's resumable design packs more interlocking state into dense steps and admits an unresolved completion gap.

author: haiku
reason: B explains the design's shape at the start, gives the stored state as an explicit field table instead of a column list inside a glossary entry, and walks every step in the same Starts/Does/Data moved/State/On failure form, so a newcomer can follow data and state through the system more easily, even though its resumable design has more parts than A's.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A is denser, but its Terms section spells out the existing primitives exactly (request limit, worker memory, attempt and retry rules, multipart part limits, signed URL limits, bucket lifecycle) and explains why each step is safe, so a newcomer gets a complete, self-contained picture; B is easier to skim but leaves more of the environment implied.

author: sonnet
reason: B is longer, but it explains every outside piece a newcomer would need: the queue's attempts, decorator and payload limits, the multipart and signed-URL calls, send_email, and where user_id comes from. It also states the rules that cover every step and the shared row reader up front, so the steps are easier to follow without knowing the stack.

author: haiku
reason: A explains the request order and why it is fixed, then covers each mechanism (atomic script, window and expiry, Retry-After from PTTL, fail-open deadline) with a stated reason, and it marks what the brief does not settle (Key Service failure, the backend timeout status) as unknown, whereas B presents its own choices, such as a 503 on Key Service failure and 'existing 502 or 504', as settled behaviour.

author: haiku
reason: A covers every request path end to end with definite behaviour, including a 503 when the Key Service fails, the plan-missing-from-config case, and a Redis-clock script that builds its own key, while B leaves the Key Service failure path undefined and spreads its mechanics across separate notes.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A is easier to follow from start to finish. Its numbered steps match the diagram, the diagram shows the cache-miss path exactly, and it says what happens in more failure cases (Key Service outage, backend refusal or timeout, Redis key loss), while B leaves those open.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives me more to understand the system with: it says why Redis is shared (otherwise 6 instances would allow 6x the limit), its diagram shows the cache-hit and cache-miss paths, its numbered steps follow the diagram, and its failure table also covers Key Service outages, backend 502/504 and lost Redis keys, with its own choices marked as not from the brief; A leaves those cases out, and B's only flaw is a small inconsistency about the Redis replica.

author: haiku
reason: A starts with the facts about today's system that an outsider lacks, such as the lint rule, the version column, scale, GDPR deletes and the empty cluster, and it describes how the system runs in each state (before and after the switch) apart from the rollout checklist; B spreads key mechanisms like erasure ordering and reverse sync across its checklist steps and depends on a more intricate lease scheme.

author: haiku
reason: B gives a newcomer the current system first (38M rows, 400 writes/s at peak, the lint rule, StaleWrite, how flags are cached, why app.jobs is not used), then walks through how writes and erasure work before and after the switch, so the design is easier to follow than A's denser lease, poll and moving control-row mechanics, even though A is tighter.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier to build a mental model from: it states today's behaviour up front, uses one write_mode flag and one symmetric sweeper instead of four flags and two relays, gives a table of where each piece of state lives, and describes the switch sequence once and reuses it for rollback. A is just as rigorous but denser, and spreads the same mechanics across more terms and special cases.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow because its summary names the three core mechanisms (version rule, outbox, fence) before the details, it explains how writes, deletes and reads behave before and after the switch in separate sections (including why a Postgres miss stops falling back to MySQL after the switch), and it walks through the switch as a T+ timeline. A is tighter and has a useful state table, but it describes mechanisms in the abstract and leaves more for the reader to piece together.
